extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary criticism; writers of poetry, prose, drama, and history
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging and producing poetry, prose, drama, romance, and historical writing — with comparisons across French, English, and Italian practice in the 17th–18th centuries. Emphasises style, unity, purpose, translation survivability, and the relationship between philosophical stance and poetic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule or standard of unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu 'neglected to give any rule or standard of unity to that immense collection of admirable political remarks and opinions which he laid before the world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large works or collections require a guiding rule or standard of unity; without it the spirit of the work 'floated hither and thither... like a ship without anchor or compass.' Anti-pattern: assembling many fine remarks without an organizing principle leads to relaxation of principle and lack of direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confining poetry to the modern and local
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The more poetry attaches itself to the present, and the life of society, the more local does it become, and subject to the influences of fashion.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If poetry limits itself to contemporary manners, witty occasional pieces, or dramatic pictures of society, it risks becoming ephemeral and 'almost impossible' to treat historically or critically. Aim for subjects and modes that grant universality and longevity rather than mere pastime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the purpose of lighter species as pastime
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The object of these productions is nothing more than to fill up the idle hours of fashionable life and amusement... their end still continues to be pastime — a thing which may be attained quite as well without poetry as with it.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing or evaluating comedies, romances for fashion, or occasional poems, treat their chief aim as entertainment. Expect that they may employ feeling or passion but are not necessarily intended to achieve higher poetic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality vs language-specific delicacy
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The beauty ... is seldom so universal. It depends very often entirely upon expression, and its delicacies, things which can be more easily felt than explained.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works whose beauty hinges on language-specific subtleties (e.g., La Fontaine) may be deeply admired by natives but resist full appreciation in translation. Prefer forms and expressions that aim at universal intelligibility when durability and international reception are priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation survivability of heroic poetry and tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A heroic poem or a tragedy can be very well comprehended although translated into a different language, and in general the greater its intrinsic excellence is, the less does it suffer by such a transmutation.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or compose epic and tragic works for strengths in fable, structure, and universal themes that survive translation; these genres are judged in part by their capacity to be transformed across languages with minimal loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy requires more than rhetoric of passion
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The rhetoric of the passions, when it forms the sole animation of the tragedy, is far from coming up to our ideas of what tragedy ought to be.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying solely on passionate rhetoric; tragedy should have structural depth, fable, and moral or philosophical weight beyond stirring expression. Anti-pattern: empty oratorical passion without substantive dramatic design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minute psychological characterization is no substitute for poetry and wit
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The psychological wire drawing of characters and passions in comedy furnishes a very unequal substitute for poetry and wit.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive analytical minuteness in character portrayal (psychologizing) can replace genuine poetic insight or comic wit; comedy benefits from liveliness and genuine humour rather than purely analytic character-sourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical materialism is inimical to poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Materialism is essentially inimical to poetry and deadening to fancy.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strongly materialist or reductive philosophical stance in a writer can blunt imaginative power and poetic feeling. When composing poetry or imaginative prose, be mindful of philosophical positions that might deaden fancy; foster beliefs or stances that preserve imaginative receptivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romance as a free vehicle vs proper narrative romance
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Romance... remained perfectly free... When Voltaire clothed his wit in this form... Rousseau embodied in it his enthusiasm... But if we regard romance as a species of poetry, and as the regular representation in narration or incidents taken from actual life and manners...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize two uses of romance: as a flexible vehicle for ideas (philosophical or moral argument) and as a narrative art-form depicting life and manners. Evaluate a romance by whether it aims to propagate ideas (may sacrifice narrative regularity) or to provide faithful, inventive representation of life (in which case unity, characterization, and fidelity to narrative form matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention and power of representation in novels
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of Richardson, Fielding, Smollett: Richardson noted for genius but false species; Fielding and Smollett excel in imitation of Cervantes; Vicar of Wakefield praised as an exquisite miniature romance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing novels, privilege invention and representational power: how convincingly and originally the narrative world and characters are created. Beware verbose or falsely-constructed species that, despite genius, are ill-suited to higher fictional aims (ascribed to Richardson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary market and genre contamination (memoirs & confessions)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘I allude to the extraordinary abundance in this literature of memoirs, confessions, books of letters and anecdotes, all more or less partaking in the nature of the romance. I am not aware that any tale of Marmontel has ever excited so universal an interest as his memoirs...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that proliferation of memoirs, confessions, and epistolary forms can displace or dilute the development of pure romance/fiction. Market tendencies shape what authors produce; judge works while accounting for genre cross-pollination and its effects on narrative quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style must suit the writer's purpose; unity of purpose and flow valued
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons: Voltaire's prose 'animated and witty' but 'in history... by no means a suitable one'; Diderot 'shews a perception ... but his language is incorrect and hasty'; Buffon fettered by his work; Rousseau praised for 'more unity of purpose, and a more eloquent flow of composition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate prose style by its fitness to purpose. Unity of purpose and eloquent, sustained composition are preferable to brilliant but ill-suited passages. Anti-patterns: incorrect or hasty language, episodic rhetoric that undermines overall effect, and stylistic choices that mismatch genre (e.g., jocular style in solemn history).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer national authenticity over foreign imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Their best means of attaining great excellence will consist, not in any strict imitation of English models, or of any foreign models whatever, but in a hearty recurrence to the old spirit and poetry of their own nation.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For revival or advancement of a nation's poetry, return to native, ancient sources and the nation's original poetic spirit rather than slavish imitation of foreign models. Authenticity fosters deeper, more appropriate development than imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Didactic poetry tends toward frigidity; needs passion to succeed
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In the original poems of Pope, we can perceive abundant traces of that predilection for thought which has rendered didactic poetry so much a favourite among the English. I have already expressed my belief, that this species contains always something of the frigid and unpoetic.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Didactic aims in poetry risk coldness and lack of lyricism; the form benefits when combined with passion, melancholy, or other genuinely poetic elements (e.g., Young). Avoid sterile instruction as the sole poetic aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive/nature poetry valued for taste and feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise of Thomson and the English passion for nature as origin of Ossian; descriptive poetry is a national favourite and often imitated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or judging descriptive poetry, value tasteful rendering of natural scenes and sincere feeling. Such works helped reawaken interest in national ballads and ancient forms; they reward sensitivity in depiction over mere didacticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic invention must be matched by musical harmony and elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: On Italian theatre: 'In Gozzi's fantastic popular stories ... we can perceive an abundance of the true poetical power of invention; but there is a great want of that musical harmony and elegance of fancy which are requisite before invention can take just possession of the stage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate drama on both invention (original plots, imagination) and on musical harmony, elegance of language, and a sense of theatrical appropriateness. A play with rich invention but without lyrical/structural elegance may fail to fully succeed on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical writing should combine freedom, originality, and knowledge of the antique
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The critical books of the English... are distinguished by greater freedom, originality, and knowledge of the antique...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary criticism and treatises should display independent thinking, openness, and classical erudition. These qualities make critical works more valuable as guides to creative practice and historical understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scepticism in historical research but not in moral/religious principles
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘However salutary the spirit of scepticism in the conduct of historical researches, I am strongly of opinion that this spirit, when it is not confined to events alone, but extends its doubts to all the principles of morality and religion, is by no means becoming in a great national historian...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historians should apply sceptical inquiry to factual claims and events, but avoid wholesale scepticism that undermines moral or religious frameworks central to national understanding. Anti-pattern: a historian whose scepticism extends to all moral principles risks diminishing influence and failing national duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historians should possess principles, feeling, and passion
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Narrow principles and views of things not perfectly just, are... much better fitted for a great historian than no principles at all, and a deadening want of feeling, warmth, and passion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate historical writing for engagement, principled perspective, and emotional warmth; these qualities create interest and make histories persuasive. A lack of feeling reduces a historian to mere paradox-making or partisan opposition without human appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid verbosity, antithesis, and excessive oratorical manner in history
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Robertson: 'too fond both of verbosity and of antithesis. The ambition of fine writing, and of the desire to treat matters in an elaborate and oratorical manner, appear to me to be extremely erroneous and out of place in a writer of history.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In historical composition prioritize research, accuracy, and substantive import over rhetorical ornament. Anti-patterns include excessive verbosity, a fondness for antithesis, and pretentious oratorical flourishes that obscure rather than illuminate events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure poetic/prose excellence by intrinsic unity and sustained eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for Rousseau over Buffon because Rousseau possesses 'more unity of purpose, and a more eloquent flow of composition in his works' even if Buffon is 'perhaps the richest and most graceful'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging writers, balance appreciation of beautiful individual passages against the unity and sustained eloquence of the whole. A coherent, flowing composition often outweighs isolated rhetorical beauties in determining lasting excellence.
